pagination_guide.overview: This guide explains how to configure pagination for REST APIs that return data across multiple pages. The connector supports 5 different pagination strategies commonly used by REST APIs.

when_to_use_pagination.criterion: API returns large datasets split across multiple pages
API documentation mentions pagination, page limits, or cursors
API responses include pagination metadata (next page, total pages, etc.)
You want to fetch ALL data, not just the first page

when_not_to_use_pagination.criterion: API returns all data in a single response
You only need the first page of results

type.name: offset
type.title: Offset-Based Pagination
type.description: Uses numeric offset and limit parameters to paginate through results. Common in SQL-based APIs.
type.how_it_works: - First request: ?offset=0&limit=100 - Second request: ?offset=100&limit=100 - Third request: ?offset=200&limit=100 - Continues until fewer than page_size results returned

type.name: page
type.title: Page-Based Pagination
type.description: Uses page numbers to paginate through results. Most common pagination type.
type.how_it_works: - First request: ?page=1&per_page=50 - Second request: ?page=2&per_page=50 - Third request: ?page=3&per_page=50 - Continues until fewer than page_size results returned

parameters.param: Query parameter name for page number (e.g., "page", "p")
Query parameter name for page size (e.g., "per_page", "limit", "size")
Starting page number (default: 1, some APIs use 0)

type.name: cursor
type.title: Cursor-Based Pagination
type.description: Uses opaque cursor tokens to paginate through results. Best for real-time data and large datasets.

parameters.param: JSON path to next cursor in response (e.g., "pagination.next_cursor", "meta.next")

type.important: The next_cursor_path uses dot notation to navigate nested JSON. Example: "pagination.next_cursor" looks for response.pagination.next_cursor Numeric array positions are written as plain numbers (e.g., "pages.0.token"). The cursor is read while the response is streamed; it may appear before or after the data. The path must not lie inside the data node ($data_path).

type.name: link_header
type.title: Link Header Pagination (RFC 5988)
type.description: Uses HTTP Link headers to provide next page URLs. Follows RFC 5988 standard.
type.how_it_works: - First request: /api/data - Response includes header: Link: ; rel="next" - Second request: Uses URL from Link header - Continues until no "next" link in header
type.important: This is the simplest pagination type - the connector automatically extracts the next page URL from the Link header. All Link header lines are read, commas inside <URI> and quoted values are handled, and relation lists such as rel="prev next" are understood. A relative URI is resolved against the URL of the page that returned it.

type.name: next_url
type.title: Next URL Pagination
type.description: API provides full URL to next page in response body. Common in hypermedia APIs.
type.how_it_works: - First request: /api/data - Response includes: {"data": [...], "pagination": {"next": "https://api.example.com/data?page=2"}} - Second request: Uses URL from response - Continues until next URL is null or missing

parameters.param: JSON path to next URL in response (e.g., "pagination.next", "links.next", "next_page")

type.important: The next_url_path uses dot notation to navigate nested JSON. The URL can be absolute or relative; a relative URL is resolved against the URL of the page that returned it. The URL is read while the response is streamed and may appear before or after the data. The path must not lie inside the data node ($data_path).

configuration_placement.rule: Place it inside the table definition, alongside $path and field definitions
Each table can have its own pagination configuration
If API doesn't use pagination, omit $pagination entirely

runtime_behavior.title: Streaming, limits and safety rules applied by the engine
runtime_behavior.rule: Responses are parsed incrementally and records are written as soon as they are complete; memory does not depend on the page size, the number of pages or the number of records.

$data_path may be a root array, a root object (one record), or a dot path such as "response.data" (numeric segments index arrays). A null data node is an empty page; a missing path or a scalar is an error.
Only objects that are direct elements of the data array are records; objects nested in other arrays are ignored.

Pagination is validated before the first request: page_size must be greater than 0 whenever limit_param is set (and for offset/page), and offset_param, page_param, cursor_param, next_cursor_path and next_url_path are required for the types that use them.
Pagination parameters replace same-named parameters already present in the request URL and are percent-encoded.

offset and page pagination stop when a page holds fewer than page_size records; with an exact multiple of page_size one extra (empty) request is made. cursor, next_url and link_header stop as soon as the server gives no continuation.
At most 10000 pages are read. If the API still announces more data at that point the request fails with an error instead of returning incomplete data.
A repeated cursor or next-page URL is treated as a pagination loop and fails the request.

Server-supplied next-page URLs and redirects must use http or https, must not contain user information and must not downgrade https to http. When authentication headers are configured, credentials are only sent to the origin (scheme, host, port) of the first request: a next-page URL on another origin is rejected, and a redirect to another origin is followed without credentials (at most 5 redirects).
Rows already written stay written if a later page or record fails: a failed request is not rolled back. A single record is never written partially.
Logs and error messages never contain query strings, cursors, tokens or response values.

example.title: Orders (Cursor-Based, cursor in response metadata)
example.note: The response looks like {"data": [...], "meta": {"next_cursor": "abc"}}. The cursor may appear before or after the data array. The cursor must be a value of its own in the response; it cannot be derived from a field of the last record, and next_cursor_path must not lie inside the data node.

issue.solution: Verify parameter names match API documentation exactly

possible_causes.cause: Wrong initial_page (should be 1 or 0 depending on API)

issue.solution: Check API documentation for starting page/offset number

possible_causes.cause: page_size too large (API may have maximum limit)

issue.solution: Reduce page_size or add rate limiting handling

best_practices.practice: Always check API documentation for pagination details
Use the largest page_size the API allows for better performance
Test pagination with APIs that have multiple pages of data
For cursor-based pagination, carefully verify the next_cursor_path
For next_url pagination, verify the next_url_path points to the correct field
Consider API rate limits when setting page_size

step.question: Does the API documentation mention pagination?

option.answer: Uses offset and limit (offset=0, offset=100, etc.)
Provides next page URL in Link HTTP header
